## Page contract — read before your first publish

These are the Artifact tool's own rules for the file you publish; the design guidance below builds on them.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Skeleton**: The file is wrapped in a `<!doctype html>…<head>…</head><body>` skeleton at publish time, so write the page content directly — no `<!DOCTYPE>`, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` tags of your own. Its head carries only a charset and viewport meta (with `viewport-fit=cover`) plus a small reset — light `color-scheme`, `:root` padded top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets, zero body margin with a 14px system font, `img{max-width:100%}`, and `[hidden]{display:none!important}` (toggle visibility with `el.hidden`, not `style.display`) — so put your own `<title>` and `<style>` at the top of the file. Keep the `:root` padding. Put `<meta name="claude:viewport-fit-sides" content="cover">` at the top of the file beside your `<title>`: it promises that the side gutter uses the two `max()` paddings given under Responsive, so the tag goes in only together with both paddings, never alone. An edit of an older page that has neither leaves both out, unless the ask redoes the page's layout. With it the page also runs under a system bar at the phone's side, where backgrounds reach that edge while the gutter keeps text and controls clear. Anything fixed to a screen edge stays at `0` and adds that edge's `env(safe-area-inset-*, 0px)` to its own padding (one that spans the width takes the side gutter too), a floating or absolutely placed control adds the nearby edges' insets to its offsets, and a sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)`, not `0`, with the band above it painted by a fixed `body::before` (`content: ""; position: fixed; inset: 0 0 auto; height: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px); z-index: 10`) in its background, or in the page's where it starts lower.

**Title**: Put a `<title>` at the top of the HTML; only the first 8KB of the file is scanned for it. It is the artifact's name in the browser tab and the gallery, so write a name, not a summary: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific enough to pick this page out among many, the way an app or a document is named. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Never use a generic category label alone, and never append an explainer after a dash or colon. If you shorten a title that pairs the name with a generic word, keep the name, not the generic word. A multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished; do not shorten it further. The explanation goes in the one-sentence `description` parameter, which becomes the gallery card's subtitle. The `title` parameter fills in only when an HTML file has no `<title>` tag (Markdown pages keep their filename). Keep the title stable across redeploys.

**External resources — CDN allowlist (CSP-enforced)**: external scripts load ONLY from https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, https://unpkg.com, https://cdn.tailwindcss.com (Tailwind's play-CDN script) and https://code.jquery.com; external stylesheets ONLY from https://fonts.googleapis.com, with the font files they pull from https://fonts.gstatic.com (give every face a real fallback stack). Everything else is blocked, with no visible error: every other host (esm.sh included) and, even on those CDNs, anything but a script — stylesheets, images, media, fetch/XHR/WebSocket, a library's runtime fetches. So inline all other CSS and JS and embed assets as data: URIs. **How to load a library**: `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/<lib>/<exact version>/<file>">` — pick the UMD build, which defines a global (e.g. react/18.3.1/umd/react.production.min.js, then react-dom) — placed BEFORE any inline `<script>` that uses it. Pin every library URL to an exact version (`react@18.3.1` on jsDelivr or unpkg, `react/18.3.1/…` on cdnjs, `cdn.tailwindcss.com/3.4.17`), never a bare name, a range or a tag (`react`, `react@18`, `@latest`). Choose a version at least two weeks old. Any version you knew before this conversation is old enough; if you look versions up, skip any published in the last two weeks. The viewer's sandbox also blocks any download the page starts itself — `<a download>` links (data:/blob: hrefs included) and script-driven saves are inert for viewers — so never offer a file through a plain link. Links to other websites (`https://…`) open in a new tab, but email, phone and app links (`mailto:`, `tel:`, `sms:`, other custom schemes) are unreliable inside an artifact: for many viewers (for example anyone outside the user's organization, or anyone viewing through a public link) following one, by link or by script, often does not work, and the page cannot tell whether it did. So show the address or number itself as selectable text (a copy button helps), treat such a link as a convenience that may do nothing, and never tell the viewer a message was sent or a call placed because the viewer tapped one. Artifacts render mermaid diagrams natively — markdown via ```mermaid fences, HTML via `<pre class="mermaid">` blocks — no library needed, don't load one. The viewer never shows `alert()`, `confirm()` or `prompt()` dialogs — `confirm()` returns false and `prompt()` returns null immediately — so build any confirmation step into the page itself.

**What the viewer's frame allows**: The page runs in a locked-down frame; what it refuses below, it refuses for every viewer (anonymous, signed-in, embedded, desktop and mobile apps), so build around these limits instead of detecting them. The page cannot open the print dialog — `window.print()` does nothing — so never offer a Print or "Save as PDF" button. Forms work as page UI (inputs, validation, submit events), but a real submission has nowhere to go: handle `submit` in script with `preventDefault()` and never point `action` at another site or a mailto: address. Copy buttons work when `navigator.clipboard.writeText` is called inside the click handler — catch its rejection (older desktop apps and some app views refuse it) and fall back to selecting the text; reading the clipboard never works, though the viewer's own Paste (the `paste` event) does. Camera, microphone, screen capture, location, motion, Web Share and similar device APIs are refused without a prompt — build on one only when this user has a runtime capability for that device (the `artifact-capabilities` skill lists them) and the page declares it; otherwise take photos, audio and data as uploaded files instead (file inputs, drag-and-drop of files and `FileReader` work in browsers). A screen wake lock may be granted while the page is visible: request it and tolerate rejection. Fullscreen and pointer lock work from a click in desktop browsers; treat both as optional (handle the rejection) since phones and some app views lack them. Sound plays only after the viewer interacts (muted autoplay is fine), so start audio from a button. Other sites cannot be embedded — no YouTube, map or form iframes, and no `<object>`/`<embed>`; link out instead: links open outside the artifact, normally in a new tab, while `window.open` works only for some signed-in viewers in the artifact's own organization and returns null for everyone else, so use real `<a href>` links. Web Workers work from your own files or `blob:` URLs; service workers and WebRTC do not. `fetch()` of files published alongside the page works with relative URLs; images from your own files, `data:` or `blob:` URLs draw to canvas and export cleanly. Only a plain `#name` passes between the artifact's link and `location.hash`, never `#/path`, `#key=value`, a `pushState` path or a query string. The address bar on the artifact's own page and Share's Copy link follow the page's hash; beside a chat, in a project or in an app the bar may not. Only where a page has several views worth bookmarking or sending, route on the hash: name each in ASCII letters, digits and hyphens (never `settings`, `sidebar`, `customize`, `upgrade`, `downloads` or `comment-*`, which claude.ai reserves) and show the one in `location.hash`, or the start view if none, on load and on `hashchange`. Keep other state in the page, and keys, tokens or private values out of the hash: it shows in history and copied links.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

**Responsive**: The page must also work at phone width (about 400px), and the page body must never scroll horizontally. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width, written `padding-left: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-left, 0px))` and `padding-right: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-right, 0px))` so that it also clears a system bar at the phone's side: set it once on `body` or one outer wrapper (where colored bands span the width, on each band's inner wrapper), and give that element its vertical padding with `padding-block`, never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Use relative units. Let flex and grid rows wrap or stack to one column when narrow, and give any flex or grid child that holds running text, code or a table `min-width: 0`, so long content wraps or scrolls inside it instead of pushing the page wider. Put `max-width: 100%` on images and on any `aspect-ratio` box, and give nothing a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only tables, diagrams and code blocks may be wider, each inside its own `overflow-x: auto` container.

**Theme-aware**: The page renders in the viewer's theme, which has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets nothing, so for most viewers only `prefers-color-scheme` tells light from dark. Define every color as a token, in this shape (token names and count are the design's own):
```css
:root { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: … }  /* every token, light values */
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme="light"]) { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark } }
:root[data-theme="dark"] { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark }  /* same dark values, so the toggle wins both ways */
body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--fg) }
```
Every token gets its first definition on bare `:root`; the two dark blocks only redefine tokens, and their `color-scheme: dark` makes form controls and scrollbars follow. No color has its only definition inside a media or `[data-theme]` block, and no component rule uses a literal color that reads in one theme only. `body` keeps that explicit token background: the viewer paints its own ground behind the page, so a transparent body shows the host's theme instead. A dark-first design mirrors the whole shape, selectors included: dark values and `color-scheme: dark` on bare `:root` (the skeleton pins `light` there), light values and `color-scheme: light` under `(prefers-color-scheme: light)` guarded `:root:not([data-theme="dark"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="light"]`. A design that deliberately commits to a single look may drop the two dark blocks but still sets the background and every color explicitly, plus `color-scheme: dark` on `:root` if that look is dark.

**Icon** (on every first publish): Pass one short generic word as `icon` (e.g. `"chart"`, `"calendar"`, `"recipe"`) for the artifact's browser-tab icon — a plain signifier for what the page is, never a product or brand name, and never an emoji or markup. It stays the **same** for the life of an artifact, so on a redeploy (the same file path this session, or `url`) omit `icon` and the artifact keeps the one it has; pass a different one only when the user asks.

Work the way the design lead at a small, versatile studio would: give each client a visual identity at the level of treatment the task calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Decide the treatment; designing is a given. A doc gets the same craft as a landing page; only the treatment differs. Format is a separate matter: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. A Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title, uses almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished, with real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages don't need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

If unsure: a well-composed page is always acceptable; an over-designed visual identity sometimes isn't.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. Follow the editorial process after them only when that reading calls for it.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Respect what already exists.** Look for an existing design system first: CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, define it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. Distinctive choices come from the subject's own world: its materials, instruments, and vernacular. Whatever the treatment, include at least one detail only this subject would have (its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art) as content rather than ornament; it costs nothing even on a plain page. Use real content throughout and never lorem ipsum.

**Pair typefaces.** Typography determines how the page reads even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the only font host the Artifact CSP allows; link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`). A face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI, or the browser silently uses a fallback. In both cases, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide. Set a type scale and keep to it. Give headings `text-wrap: balance`, give body text comfortable spacing, and give uppercase labels a little letter-spacing.

**Load libraries instead of inlining them.** When the page really needs a library (React, a charting or highlighting package), load its UMD build from cdnjs with one `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">`, pinned to an exact version at least two weeks old and placed before the inline script that uses its global; don't inline the library's source or hand-write a substitute. Only the script loads this way; a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined, and the page contract above lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images, and its data ship with the page. Most pages don't need any library; use one only when it does substantial work for the page.

**Choose neutrals deliberately.** A pure mid-grey looks unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent looks intentional. Pure white and near-black are fine backgrounds when they suit the subject, as long as you chose the neutral deliberately instead of inheriting a default.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets *nothing*. Most viewers see the document with no `data-theme` attribute, where only `prefers-color-scheme` distinguishes light from dark. Structure the CSS at the token level for all three. The bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice overrides a dark OS setting; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also overrides in the other direction; wherever the dark palette applies - both dark blocks, or bare `:root` in a dark-first or single-dark design - also set `color-scheme: dark` (the skeleton pins `light` on `:root`), so native form controls and scrollbars follow the palette. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block: a color defined only inside `[data-theme]` never applies when no `data-theme` attribute is set, and the page then shows one theme's text on the other theme's background. Two more rules keep each theme consistent. First, the artifact is composited over a background the viewer paints in *its own* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token; a transparent body shows the host's background with no warning. Second, every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never from a literal that works in only one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it; a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first: don't simply invert it; keep contrast legible and keep the accent working on both backgrounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme: then omit the media query and `[data-theme]` blocks entirely but still set the background and every color explicitly, so the page looks right on either host background; do this by choice, never by omission.

**Use layout for spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap` instead of per-element margins, which collapse or double without warning. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width, written `padding-left: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-left, 0px))` and `padding-right: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-right, 0px))` so that it also clears a system bar at the phone's side: set it once on `body` or one outer wrapper (where colored bands span the width, on each band's inner wrapper), whose vertical padding uses `padding-block` and never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (about 400px). Give images and any `aspect-ratio` box `max-width: 100%`, and don't give anything a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only wide tables, code, and diagrams may exceed it; give each `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. The publish skeleton pads `:root` top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets (zero everywhere except a phone app) so the page runs edge to edge while its content stays clear of the system bars; keep that padding. Put `<meta name="claude:viewport-fit-sides" content="cover">` at the top of the file beside your `<title>`: it promises that the side gutter uses those two `max()` paddings, so the tag goes in only together with both paddings, never alone. An edit of an older page that has neither leaves both out, unless the ask redoes the page's layout. With it the page also runs under a system bar at the phone's side. Anything fixed to a screen edge stays at `0` and adds that edge's inset to its own padding (one that spans the width takes the side gutter too); a floating or absolutely placed control adds the nearby edges' insets to its offsets. A sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` and never `0`. So that nothing scrolls into view above it, under the host's controls, paint that band with `body::before { content: ""; position: fixed; inset: 0 0 auto; height: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px); z-index: 10; background: ... }`, in the header's own background where the header opens the page and in the page's where the sticky bar starts lower. Size a one-screen app with `height: 100%` on `html` and `body` instead of `100vh`, so it fits inside the `:root` padding. A page that includes its own viewport meta gets the `:root` padding only when that meta declares `viewport-fit=cover`. Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Make repeated elements consistent.** For cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, or badges on sibling items, use the same edges, baselines, and inner padding on each, and put any recurring element in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over empty space or sits alone in a row. Make text that can outgrow its track wrap or scroll in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Use card styling selectively.** Border, fill, radius, and shadow each mark an element as a separate object. Apply them by role, to set off the one element that needs it; applying the same radius and shadow to every block flattens the hierarchy. Open with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to scale.** Place marks, ticks, and labels with one scale, and make every label name a value the chart actually reaches. Color chart text from the theme tokens so it is readable in both themes. Keep marks, labels, and edges clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds; in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Make the page complete at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, with no scrolling to trigger it; that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all see. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never left at `opacity: 0` waiting for an observer. Size a hero to its content instead of to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the rest of the page out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state: the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, or a plausibly filled form, clearly marked as examples and never presented as the user's own figures. The first view shows what the tool does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing. When those records live in the `db` capability, keep them out of the page source. Its first frame renders before the store answers, so make that frame a designed empty state that names what will appear and how to add the first entry, then fill it from the store. Seed the store through the `ArtifactData` tool (what type instructions call `write_db`) after the first publish: the user's real data, or marked examples for a tool only the user will use. For a store other people will fill with their own entries, seed only what the user gave you or asked for, never invented people or records.

**Avoid AI-generated design.** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. When the user specifies a visual direction, follow it exactly; their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. When nothing is specified, don't use that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly.** Watch for overlapping elements, cascade collisions, and silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, and respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform preserves form values, focus, and scroll position across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, use Canvas or WebGL instead of hand-writing long SVG path data.

**CSS rules.** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificity. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out, e.g. a type-based selector like `.section` and an element-based one like `.cta` both setting padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't undo your spacing unnoticed.

**Writing the copy.** Treat words as design material and never as decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen: name things by what people recognize instead of how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*; they don't manage *webhook config*). Use active voice; a control states exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it, without apologies or vagueness. Prefer specific to clever. Write plainly, the way a knowledgeable person would talk. Avoid mannered devices: asides set off by em-dashes, "not X, but Y" framing, colon-then-reveal sentences, scare quotes around invented labels, and stock phrases such as "worth noting" or "honest caveat". Prefer short, direct sentences over compressed or clever phrasing.

**Name the page like a product; don't caption it.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it gives the reader a first impression of the care taken. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject; or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which then is the page's name. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Stop at the name; a title that adds its own explanation after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it appears beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could apply to any of them fails as a name just as an appended explanation does. When a candidate title combines the name with a generic word (a greeting, a category, a page-type label), keep the name; a trim that drops the identifying part and keeps the generic word produces a title that could apply to any page. This rule removes explanations and doesn't require brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. Put the explanation in the one-sentence publish `description`; the gallery shows it directly under the title.

**Structure is information.** Structural devices (numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels) should encode something true about the content instead of decorating it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but those fit only if the content actually is a sequence, such as a real process or a typed timeline where the order is information the reader needs. Before adding numbered markers or similar devices, check that they actually make sense.

**When the page is a UI (dashboard, tool).** It is scanned and operated instead of read top to bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Put the summary before the detail. Encode state in form as well as in numbers (a pill, a chip, a severity stripe) so that whatever needs attention is visible at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. Interactive elements should look interactive.



## Process

Start from what the viewer should be able to do on the page, in addition to what they will read. If the page should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user. A page that is only read doesn't need that.

Before writing the page, settle a short design plan (a compact token system) and write it into the file itself, as the `:root` block at the top of the page's `<style>`, rather than into your reply:
- **Color**: the palette as 4-6 named color tokens.
- **Type**: font tokens for 2+ roles: a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: the layout concept as a one-line comment above the tokens.

Then build the rest of the page from those tokens, deriving every color and type decision from them. The plan is working material, not part of the answer: unless the user asks about the design, one plain sentence on the direction is the most to say about it, with no hex values or font names.

**Write, check once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once, where this session offers a way: one `ArtifactCheck` preview (or the Artifact tool's own `action: "preview"` where there is no separate `ArtifactCheck` tool), or else one screenshot of the local file; if the session offers none of these, skip the look. The preview renders desktop and phone widths in light and dark and lists overflow, colors that ignore the theme, blocked loads and console errors, including a script that fails to parse, so nothing it covers needs a check of your own. The look is optional: if you take it, make one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look; then publish. For a page that charts real numbers, take the look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. A page whose point is logic (dates, money, scoring, parsing) may get one more check before publishing: one run of a pure function on a sample input, or, where no preview ran, one syntax check of its script; nothing more. A page that declares `capabilities` takes the look rather than skipping it, then one functional pass after the first publish, because the preview cannot run that code: read back once what the page stores or serves (one read of its stored data or one read-only route call; where that read alone would prove nothing, as on an empty store, you may first write one probe document yourself and delete it after the read, passing the `version` the write returned as `if_version`; no other test writes unless the user wants one), tell the user in one line what you exercised and what you could not, and stop. None of this becomes a loop, because the user is waiting for a link: no second screenshot, no scripts that probe the DOM, no re-running a check that passed. Review happens on the live page, and further polish is for the user to request; if the user reports something visibly broken (a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing), fix that, take at most one more look if the session offers a way, and republish once. These checks are for code you wrote into this page, not for content you fill into an Artifact made from an Artifact type (a Slides deck, a Design canvas): there the type's own instructions say whether to check, and if they say nothing, don't.

**Open viewers.** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open: published changes are delivered to them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state preserved where possible. If your page has state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`; `hot` is the viewer's own update hook, not a capability behind `claude.use()`, and is absent outside a viewer, hence the `?.`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance changes here: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated decisions, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part in the plan itself, without narrating the revision to the user. Write the code only after the plan is specific to this subject, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero states the thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world (headline, image, live demo, interactive moment). 
- Typography sets the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, avoiding the families you would use on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design instead of a neutral container for the content. 
- Use motion deliberately. Think about whether and where animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. One orchestrated moment is usually more effective than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation adds to the impression that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Put your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent clashes with the background, shift it toward an analogous hue or desaturate it instead of replacing it.

input.content:
Maester 3.0 · report shell · proposal

Report navigation with hubs

The left menu on the overview keeps only the pages that cover the whole run, plus one row for each hub: Products, Frameworks and each installed pack. Selecting a hub opens its own menu, as a resource menu does in the Azure portal. The home menu shrinks to an icon rail beside it, so you can jump to another hub without going back. Click around the frame below; it is example data from the Pora Inc. sample report.

Try: Zero Trust › Identity, then the rail to jump to Products.
Maester
Report · Pora Inc. · 2 Nov 2026
Search tests, controls, pages⌘K

How it behaves

  • Two levels, never three. The home menu lists pages and hubs. A hub's menu lists pages. Anything deeper (a lane, a test) is on the page or in the flyover.
  • Rows with a chevron open a hub; rows without one open a page. Opening a hub also opens its first page, so a click always changes what you see.
  • On a desktop the home menu folds into an icon rail while a hub is open. Hover shows the name, a red dot marks failures, and a click goes straight to that page or hub.
  • On a phone the menu is a drawer. A hub slides in over the home menu with a back row, and there is no rail.
  • The URL decides the menu. #/pack/zta/plan/identity opens with the Zero Trust menu and Identity selected, so links and reloads land in the same place. Back and Esc go up a level.
  • Breadcrumbs above each page title show the hub and page (Report › Zero Trust › Identity) and let you go up.
  • A hub menu with more than about twelve rows gets a filter box, as Azure's resource menu does. ⌘K still searches every page and test.

What changes on today's pages

  • Home menu: from about 30 rows on a full run to about 12. The Products and Frameworks lists, the folding groups and the remembered fold state go away.
  • Zero Trust plan: the pillar tabs (Identity 114, Devices 142…) move into the hub menu. The Swimlanes and Table switch stays on the page, because it changes how one pillar is shown rather than which page is open.
  • Pack page: its "Group tests by" control stays. The hub also lists one page per value of the pack's first field (ZTA: Pillar), which is today's grouping with a link of its own.
  • Embedded reports (the Zero Trust Assessment HTML) move from the global Reports group into their pack's hub. Run details stays on the home menu.
  • Several tenants: All tenants stays on top. Each tenant becomes a hub row whose menu is that tenant's home menu, so the structure is the same with one tenant or many.
  • Old links (#/zero-trust, #/product/entra) keep working. They redirect to the new paths, and the product and framework paths don't change at all.

How a pack adds its own menu

A pack describes its menu in maester-pack.json, under a new Report key. It can only point at views the report already knows how to draw. A pack can't ship script into the report: the report is one self-contained file people email around, and running a pack's code in it would mean trusting every pack with whatever the report holds.

"Report": {
  "Title": "Zero Trust",
  "Navigation": [
    { "Title": "Overview", "View": "pack" },
    { "Section": "Zero Trust plan", "View": "plan", "Attachment": "zero-trust-workshop", "Expand": "pillars" },
    { "Section": "Results", "Items": [
        { "Title": "All tests", "View": "tests" },
        { "Title": "Not met", "View": "tests", "Result": "Failed" } ] },
    { "Section": "Results by pillar", "View": "tests", "GroupBy": "Pillar" },
    { "Section": "Reports", "View": "attachment", "Attachment": "zero-trust-assessment" },
    { "Title": "About this pack", "View": "about" }
  ]
}
ViewDrawsTakes
packThe pack's overview: tiles, top failures, its bannernothing
testsThe pack's tests, as on All tests. With GroupBy, one row per value of a field.GroupBy, Result, Filter on Fields
planA JSON attachment drawn by a renderer the report ships, picked by the attachment's schema (today maester.zero-trust-workshop/1). Expand asks the renderer for one row per pillar.Attachment, Expand
attachmentAn HTML or Markdown attachment in the page frame (as Reports does today)Attachment
guideA page from the pack's maester-pack.guide.jsonPage
aboutPublisher, version, licence, the permissions the pack used, linksnothing

A pack that declares nothing still gets a hub: Overview, one page per value of its first field, a page per attachment, and About. The example "Contoso baseline" pack in the frame shows this default. A new kind of page (another plan format, say) is a renderer added to the report in Maester, and any pack can then use it.

Maester builds the Products and Frameworks hubs from the same hub structure, so the shell has one way to draw every menu.

Hubs and their menus

HubMenuPath
ProductsOne row per product that ran, with failures#/product/entra
FrameworksOne row per framework, then MITRE ATT&CK#/framework/cis-m365
Each packWhat the pack declares, or the default#/pack/<code>/<page>
Each tenant (merged runs)That tenant's home menu#/t/<tenant>/…

Decisions before I build it

  1. Rail beside the hub menu on desktop (Azure style, as in the frame) or a plain drill-in everywhere (the phone behaviour on every screen)? I recommend the rail: you can move between hubs in one click and still see where you are.
  2. Products and Frameworks as hubs, or left on the home menu as folding lists? As hubs they cut the home menu the most. The cost is one more click to reach a product.
  3. The pack Report.Navigation schema: start with these six views and the default for packs that declare nothing, and add to it when a pack needs more?
  4. The Zero Trust plan path: move it under the pack (#/pack/zta/plan/identity) and redirect #/zero-trust/… to it?

The top half is a clickable copy of the report with a Desktop/Phone switch. I checked the script for syntax errors but haven't clicked through the live page yet.

**How the left menu works:**
- **Overview:** the menu shrinks from about 30 rows to about 12:
  - Overview, Action plan, Changes, All tests and Affected objects.
  - A **Products ›** row and a **Frameworks ›** row.
  - A **Packs** section with one row per pack (Zero Trust ›).
  - Run details at the bottom.
- **Opening a hub:** a chevron means the row opens a hub. The hub's own menu slides in and its first page opens. On a desktop, the home menu folds into an icon rail beside it, like the Azure portal, so you can jump to another hub in one click. A red dot on the rail marks failures.
- **Zero Trust hub:** the menu has:
  - Overview.
  - **Zero Trust plan** with one row per pillar and a small progress bar. These replace the pillar tabs on the page.
  - **Results** (All tests, Not met).
  - **Reports** (the assessment's HTML report, moved out of the global Reports group).

- **Swimlanes/Table switch:** it stays on the page, because it changes how one pillar is shown, not which page is open.

content.text:
You're right, a hard two-level limit doesn't work for packs, so I've changed the rule. Version 2 of the mock is at the same link: https://claude.ai/artifact/D2JsAWQ8a9421cHwFZrgxC

**Two columns, any depth.** I picked two levels to keep the rail and the phone drawer simple, and that only needs a limit on columns, not on depth. There are still only two columns: the home menu (or its rail) and one hub menu. Anything below a hub is an expandable tree inside the hub menu:
- **Arrow and name do different things:** the arrow expands a row in place, and clicking the name opens that row's page.
- **Example:** the mock shows Zero Trust › Identity › Access control › Conditional Access, which is four levels. The rail, the back row and the phone drawer work the same at every depth.
- **Breadcrumbs** show the whole path, and each part opens its page.
- **The tree follows the page:** opening a page from a link or search expands its parents, so the selected row is always visible.
- **Pack schema:** depth comes three ways, and they can be mixed:
  - any entry can hold `Items` to any depth;
  - `GroupBy` with several fields nests the groups (Pillar, then Category);
  - `Expand` with several levels nests the rows a renderer adds (pillars, then areas, then swimlanes).

**Expand and collapse:**
- **Collapse to the rail:** the panel button in the top bar or at the top of the menu, or the `[` key, folds the menu to the icon rail, on the overview and in hubs.
- **Hubs while collapsed:** selecting a hub on the collapsed rail opens its menu as a flyover over the page. Picking a page, clicking the page or pressing Esc closes it. **Keep open** brings the menu back.
- **Resize:** drag the menu's right edge to widen it for deep trees (200 to 380px). Double-click the edge to reset it.
- **Remembered per viewer:** the browser keeps the collapsed state and the width, not the report file.

I clicked through the tree, collapse, the flyover, Keep open and expand on a local copy before publishing.

I've added one decision to the list on the page: whether to limit depth. I recommend no hard limit in the report, with pack validation warning past five levels. Each level indents the menu, so labels get shorter.
Build it

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.


Summary:
1. **Primary Request and Intent:**
   - **Earlier work (done, uncommitted):** the Zero Trust Workshop view in the Maester report.
     - Option A's swimlane board is the default view at `#/zero-trust/<pillar>`; the table is at `/table`.
     - Tasks open in a flyover.
     - The workshop data is bundled in the ZTA pack.
     - The custom diagram was removed.
   - **"the site is not up yet"** and **"can you start it again":** restart the dev server. Done both times: zt-report on port 5175, because 5174 is taken. The server seems to stop when the session goes idle.
   - **Left nav redesign (latest focus):** "the Azure blade based left nav is something we should think of implementing. so when I pick zero trust we then have the second level nav that shows the sub options. can you come up with an overall design and how the packs can introduce their own navigation etc. plus i want to make the left nav more cleaner at the home page so when we click we can drill down in. make a mock of how it will work and the design and let me know before building it".
   - **Follow-ups:**
     - "why are we saying onyl two levels. i think to make it expandable (maybe if the pack wants to have more laywers we should allow).."
     - "we also need the user to have the option to exapnd and collapse the left bars if they want..."
   - **Don't build until approved.** The user must approve the mock first.

2. **Key Technical Concepts:**
   - **Report app:** React with Preact compat, Vite singlefile, a hash router and `mt-` CSS classes.
     - `buildViews()` in `report/src/components/report/views.ts` builds a `ViewDef[]` with groups Tenants, Summary, Products, Frameworks, Packs and Reports.
     - The `Sidebar` in `Shell.tsx` renders the groups, folds them (stored in localStorage as `mt-nav-folded`) and shows "+ Add a pack".
     - Pack views come from the rows' `Fields`. `/zero-trust` is added when the workshop attachment exists.
     - ZT page has pillar tabs (`mt-zt-pillars`) and a Swimlanes/Table segment.
   - **Pack manifest:** `packs/zero-trust-assessment/maester-pack.json` has Id `maester.zero-trust-assessment` and Code `ZTA`. The pack attaches JSON via `Add-MtReportAttachment -Name 'zero-trust-workshop' -ContentType 'application/json'`.
   - **Proposed nav design (the mock):**
     - **Home menu:** Overview, Action plan, Changes since last run, All tests, Affected objects. Then hub rows: Products ›, Frameworks ›, a Packs section (Zero Trust ›, Contoso baseline ›) with "+ Add a pack", and Run details.
     - **Hubs:** opening a hub opens its first page. On desktop the home menu folds into a 52px icon rail (red dot for failures) beside the hub menu (236px). On phone it's a drawer that drills in with a back row and no rail.
     - **Two columns, any depth:** deeper levels are an expandable tree in the hub menu. The arrow toggles a row; its label opens that row's page. The example is Zero Trust › Identity › Access control › Conditional Access.
     - **Opening a page** expands its parents. Breadcrumbs show the full path.
     - **Collapse:** the panel button, top-bar button or `[` collapses the menu to the rail. A hub picked on the collapsed rail opens as a peek flyover. Picking a page, clicking the page or pressing Esc closes it; "Keep open" pins the menu back.
     - **Resize:** drag the menu edge between 200 and 380 px; double-click resets. The state is kept in the viewer's localStorage.
     - **Filter box** in hub menus with more than about 12 rows.
     - **URL decides the menu,** for example `#/pack/zta/plan/identity`. Old links redirect.
   - **Pack contract:** a `Report.Navigation` key in `maester-pack.json` that points only at built-in views. There's no pack JavaScript in the report, for security, because the report is a self-contained file.
     - The views: `pack`, `tests` (with `GroupBy` as a list of fields that nests, `Result` and `Filter`), `plan` (renderer chosen by the attachment schema, `Expand: ["pillars","areas","lanes"]`), `attachment`, `guide` (with `Page`) and `about`.
     - Any entry can hold `Items`, to any depth.
     - **Default when a pack declares nothing:** Overview, one page per value of the first field, attachments, and About.
     - Products and Frameworks hubs use the same hub structure.
   - **Open decisions listed in the mock:**
     1. Rail beside the hub menu vs a plain drill-in everywhere. I recommend the rail.
     2. Products and Frameworks as hubs vs folding lists.
     3. Start the pack schema with the six views.
     4. Depth limit: I recommend no hard limit, with pack validation warning past five levels.
     5. Move the ZT path to `#/pack/zta/plan/identity` and redirect `#/zero-trust/…` to it.

3. **Files and Code Sections:**
   - **Mock:** `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-merill-github-maester/9bc9d96b-2b79-4851-80f9-ab9184d1fb1a/scratchpad/report-nav/maester-report-nav.html`
     - Published as https://claude.ai/artifact/D2JsAWQ8a9421cHwFZrgxC. Version 2 is labelled "Nested menus, collapse and resize". Icon: layout.
     - Vanilla JS, using the report's tokens with dark mode.
     - **State:** `st = { hub, id, phone, drawer, dir, filter, view, open: Set, collapsed, peek, menuW }`, with load and save under localStorage `mt-nav`.
     - **Functions:** `walk`/`findItem` return `{it, hub, trail}`, plus `matches`, `treeHtml(it, depth, q, sibKids)`, `itemHtml(it, depth)`, `groupsHtml`, `railHtml` (with an expand button when collapsed), `renderNav` (`mtools` row with back/eyebrow, a collapse or "Keep open" button, `.menuwrap` and `.grip`), `renderMain` (kinds: overview, list, plan, embed, about), `go(id)` (expands the trail, clears peek), `openHub` (sets peek when collapsed), `up`, `setCollapsed`.
     - **Handlers:** data-tw, data-collapse (`setCollapsed(!st.peek)`), data-expand, data-hub, data-id, data-up, data-view and menubtn (drawer on phone, collapse on desktop). A click on main closes peek. Esc and `[` are handled. Pointer drag on `.grip` resizes; dblclick resets.
     - **Data:** HOME, HUBS (products, frameworks, zt, cb), AREAS per pillar, with lanes under identity › access.
     - **Notes sections:** How it behaves; What changes on today's pages; How a pack adds its own menu (JSON plus a views table); Hubs and their menus; Decisions before I build it.

A module the user installs themselves can only be run in a separate process: `{ "Name": "X", "MinimumVersion": "2.0.0", "Install": "User", "Process": "Child" }`. |
| `Requires.Packs` | Other packs this one needs: `{ "Id": "contoso.base", "Source": "contoso/maester-base", "Version": ">=1.0" }`. They are installed first, with their own approval. |
| `Exports` | Functions of this pack that packs requiring it may call. |

| `EnabledByDefault` | For a pack that ships with Maester: `false` to leave it off until the config turns it on. |

```

Maester checks that the Guide is a JSON object and that its screenshots (at most six) are `.png`, `.jpg` or `.webp`
paths inside the pack. Like the banner, a screenshot that really is an image of at most 1 MB is not counted as
binary content. Any section can end with `"More": "<https link>"` to your own documentation. The
[Zero Trust Assessment pack's guide](https://github.com/maester365/maester/blob/main/packs/zero-trust-assessment/maester-pack.guide.json)
is a full example.

## Tests and helpers
`ZeroTrustAssessment.ReportPath` (see [Read a report you already have](#read-a-report-you-already-have-recommended-in-ci)).
Maester's step can then connect any way it likes, including OIDC, as long as it is the same tenant.

## The assessment's own report

The Maester report embeds the HTML report the assessment wrote, with its pillar dashboards and charts. Open it
with the **Zero Trust Assessment** button on the report's overview, under **Reports** in the left menu, or on any
ZTA result. It opens inside the Maester report, with an option to open it in a new browser tab, and works
offline, so the Maester report stays a single file to share.

The embedded report is compressed: a 10 MB assessment report adds about 2 MB to the Maester report. It is left
out when `ZeroTrustAssessment.EmbedReport` is `false`, when you read a report file that has no
`ZeroTrustAssessmentReport.html` beside it or one folder up, and when `Invoke-Maester -RedactUserIdentity` is
used, because Maester cannot redact the assessment's report.

## Zero Trust plan

The report's **Zero Trust plan** view shows the [Microsoft Zero Trust Workshop](https://zerotrust.microsoft.com)
plan for the tenant. Each pillar (Identity, Devices, Data, Network, Infrastructure, Security Operations and AI) is
split into functional areas and swimlanes, and each task has its phase, priority, effort, user impact, licence,
dependencies and Microsoft's guidance. A task shows the status of the checks that measure it, so you can see which
parts of the plan are done, which fail and which no check covers yet. The pillars the run has results for are marked.

The view opens on **Swimlanes**: one functional area at a time, with its swimlanes as rows and the workshop's phases
(First, Then, Next) as columns. **Table** lists every task in the pillar, grouped by functional area and swimlane,
and can be sorted and filtered. Select a task in either view to see its checks and guidance in a panel on the right.

A task's checks come from three places:

- the assessment tests Microsoft maps to the task;
- Maester's built-in tests that check the same setting as one of those assessment tests;
- Maester tests that Maester maps to the task itself, with a note where it checks more than the workshop asks.

Maester also adds a few tasks the workshop does not have, such as hardening Microsoft Entra Connect sync. They are
marked as Maester's. Run Maester's own tests with the pack (`Invoke-Maester -Pack ZTA`) to see their status.

The new menu is built and works in the report the way the mock showed it. I clicked through it in the browser, the report builds, and all 7,047 unit tests pass. Nothing is committed.

**What changed in the report**
- **Home menu:** it lists only Overview, Action plan, Changes, All tests and Affected objects, then a row each for Products, Frameworks and every pack, then reports and Run details. The folding groups are gone.
- **Hubs:** selecting one opens its menu beside the icon rail, which marks failures with red dots. Hub menus are trees of any depth, and a page's parents expand when you open it. Breadcrumbs show the full path.
- **Example:** the Zero Trust pack's menu goes four levels deep (Identity › Users and Groups › Passwordless). Choosing an area or swimlane scrolls to the board, and a swimlane shows only that lane.
- **Collapse:**
  - The panel button, the top-bar menu button or `[` collapses the menu to the rail.
  - A hub picked on the collapsed rail opens as a flyover. Esc, clicking the page or picking a page closes it; **Keep open** brings the menu back.
- **Resize:** drag the menu's edge between 200 and 380 px, and double-click it to reset. The collapsed state and width are kept in the viewer's browser.
- **Filter:** hub menus with more than 12 rows get a filter box.
- **Phone:** the menu is a drawer that drills into a hub, with a back row and no rail.
- **Zero Trust pages:**
  - The plan moved to `#/pack/zta/plan/<pillar>/<area>/<lane>`.
  - The table view is now `#table` on the same address.
  - Old `#/zero-trust/…` links redirect.
  - The pillar tabs are gone, because the menu replaces them.

**How a pack declares its menu**
- **Manifest key:** `Report.Navigation` in `maester-pack.json`, using six built-in views: `pack`, `tests`, `plan`, `attachment`, `guide` and `about`.
- **Nesting:** `Items` to any depth, `GroupBy` with several fields, or `Expand` with several levels.
- **Validation:** Maester refuses a malformed entry. An unknown view and a menu more than five levels deep are warnings, as you decided.
- **No code from packs:** the report draws only its own views, so a pack never adds code to the report file.
- **Packs with no menu** get an overview, one page per value of their first field, their reports, the guide pages if they have a guide, and About. The ZTA pack now declares its own menu.
- **Deep menus survive:** the result JSON is written at depth 5, so `Get-MtResultPack` carries the menu and guide as JSON text to keep nested menus intact.
- **Docs and tests:** I added a section to [writing-a-pack.md](website/docs/packs/writing-a-pack.md), added `Report` to the published schema, and updated the ZTA docs and the unit tests.

**Before you merge**
- `ZeroTrustAssessmentPack.Tests.ps1` ran as part of `pester.ps1` (16.5 s, passed). It ran in a fresh PowerShell with no tenant connection, so it couldn't reach a tenant. If you want the full suite to skip it, it needs excluding there.
- The **Assessment report** row only appears in a real ZTA run, because the dev sample has no HTML attachment, so I haven't seen it.
- `report/src/components/report/views.ts` is deleted. The new code is in [nav.ts](report/src/components/report/nav.ts), [Sidebar.tsx](report/src/components/report/Sidebar.tsx) and [PackRoute.tsx](report/src/pages/report/PackRoute.tsx).

result.output:
## Quick start

Prefer to click through the choices? The [test builder](/test-builder) explains every attribute and
writes the code for you.

```powershell
# 1. Create custom/Test.CONTOSO.1001.ps1 and custom/Test.CONTOSO.1001.md
New-MtTest -Id CONTOSO.1001 -Title 'Guest invitations are restricted' -Service Graph -Severity High `
    -Product entra -Feature external-identities -Area external-access

# 2. Edit the two files, then check them. No tenant connection is needed for this step.
Get-MtTest -Path ./custom

# 3. Run the test on its own while you write it
Connect-Maester
Invoke-MtTest -Path ./custom/Test.CONTOSO.1001.ps1

# 4. Run it with everything else
Invoke-Maester -Path .
```

`New-MtTest` writes to `./custom` unless you pass `-Path`. It supports `-WhatIf` and refuses to overwrite
existing files unless you pass `-Force`. Only `-Id` and `-Title` are required; `-Product`, `-Feature`, `-Area`,
`-ResourceType`, `-UserImpact`, `-ImplementationCost` and `-Mitre` fill in the attributes of the same name.

## Files and layout

Put your tests in a folder of your own, usually `custom/` inside the folder you run Maester from:

```text
maester/
  maester-config.json        (optional: your run configuration)
  custom/
    Test.CONTOSO.1001.ps1
    Test.CONTOSO.1001.md
    suite.json               (optional: name, tags and source for every test in the folder)
    maester-config.json      (optional: an overlay on the root config)
```

`Invoke-Maester -Path ./maester` finds every `Test.*.ps1` file under the path, in any subfolder up to three
levels deep (`./maester/a/b/c/Test.CONTOSO.1001.ps1`). If you leave out `-Path`, Maester looks for custom
tests only in the `custom` folder of the current folder, and reads the config files of the current folder. Without
a `custom` folder only the built-in tests run.

Pester-format tests (`*.Tests.ps1`) must be in a `custom` folder: `-Path` itself, or a `custom` folder under it.
See [Pester-format tests](./pester-format-tests.md).

Maester matches the `custom` folder name without regard to case, so a `Custom` folder created by Maester 2.x keeps
working, and `New-MtTest` writes into it when it exists.

Rules for a test file:

- The file name is `Test.<ID>.ps1`, where `<ID>` is the `Id` in the attribute. The `.md` file has the same
  name with the `.md` extension and sits in the same folder. A custom test without its `.md` file is reported
  as `Error` with reason `InvalidMetadata`.
- The file contains exactly one function with a `[MaesterTest(...)]` attribute. It may contain other functions
  (helpers, or a family's instance source).
- At the top level the file contains only function definitions: no statements, no script-level `param()`
  block. Discovery never executes the file, and this rule keeps it that way.
- The test function has `[CmdletBinding()]`.

### Test IDs

An ID is letters and digits in segments separated by `.` or `-` (and `_` after the first segment). It starts
with a letter, contains at least one digit or separator, and is at most 64 characters. `CONTOSO.1001`,
`CONTOSO-ID-07` and `CT0001` are all valid. IDs are compared case-insensitively.

A test that implements a benchmark requirement is named after it: the suite's prefix, then the requirement's
ID as the benchmark writes it, without a version suffix. That is also its `Id` in the framework file. The prefix ends in a period;
the rest keeps the benchmark's own punctuation, so a reader can search for the ID the benchmark uses.

| Test ID | Prefix | The benchmark's ID |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CIS.M365.5.2.2.2` | `CIS.M365.` | Recommendation `5.2.2.2` of the CIS Microsoft 365 Foundations Benchmark |
| `CISA.MS.AAD.3.1` | `CISA.` | SCuBA policy `MS.AAD.3.1v1`, without its version suffix |
| `ASD.ISM-1504` | `ASD.` | ISM control `ISM-1504`, written with a hyphen by ASD |

Use a prefix of your own. These prefixes belong to the tests that ship with Maester: `MT.`, `CISA.`, `CIS.`,
`EIDSCA.`, `ORCA.`, `AD-`, `AZDO.`, `ASD.` and `MT1060.`. `MP.` is reserved for Maester Packs, third-party test packs
planned for a later release. A custom test with one of these prefixes still runs, with a
warning. A custom test that uses the exact ID of a built-in test is not run at all, and the built-in runs
instead. To change how a built-in test behaves, set its parameters or severity in the
[run configuration](../configuration/run-configuration.md), or copy it under your own ID and disable the
built-in.

Two native tests with the same ID (or the same function name) both get an `Error` row with reason
`DuplicateId`, and neither runs. When a native test and a Pester-format test share an ID, the native test
runs and the Pester test does not; it is listed under `Selection.Superseded` in the result with `MatchedBy`
`NativeTest`.

## A complete example

`custom/Test.CONTOSO.1002.ps1`:

```powershell
function Test-ContosoDisabledCaPolicyReason {
    [MaesterTest(
        Id           = 'CONTOSO.1002',
        Title        = 'Disabled Conditional Access policies state why they are disabled.',
        Product      = 'entra',
        Feature      = 'conditional-access',
        Area         = 'access-control',
        ResourceType = 'ConditionalAccessPolicy',
        Severity     = 'Medium',
        Service      = 'Graph',
        License      = 'AAD_PREMIUM',
        Tag          = 'Contoso'
    )]
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([bool])]
    param(
        # Text that a disabled policy's name must contain.
        [string] $ReasonMarker = 'Disabled:'
    )

    $policies = Get-MtConditionalAccessPolicy
    $withoutReason = @($policies | Where-Object { $_.state -eq 'disabled' -and $_.displayName -notlike "*$ReasonMarker*" })

    if ($withoutReason.Count -eq 0) {
        Add-MtTestResultDetail -Result 'Well done. Every disabled policy states why it is disabled.'
        return $true
    }

    $result = "These disabled policies do not state why they are disabled:`n`n%TestResult%"
    Add-MtTestResultDetail -Result $result -GraphObjects $withoutReason -GraphObjectType ConditionalAccess
    return $false
}
```

`custom/Test.CONTOSO.1002.md`:

```md
Disabled Conditional Access policies must say why they are disabled, in the form `Disabled: <reason>`.

#### Remediation action

1. In the Microsoft Entra admin center, open **Protection** > **Conditional Access** > **Policies**.
2. For each policy listed below, add the reason to its name, or delete the policy.

#### Related links

- [Conditional Access policies](https://entra.microsoft.com/#view/Microsoft_AAD_ConditionalAccess/ConditionalAccessBlade/~/Policies)

<!--- Results --->
%TestResult%
```

There is no connection check, no licence check and no `try`/`catch` in the function. The engine does all three.

## The `[MaesterTest]` attribute
## What the function returns

| The function does | Result | Reason code |
| --- | --- | --- |
| returns `$true` | `Passed` | |
| returns `$false` | `Failed` | |
| calls `Add-MtTestResultDetail -Investigate` | `Investigate`, whatever it returns | |
| calls `Add-MtTestResultDetail -SkippedBecause <code>` | `Skipped`. The call ends the test. | `TestSkipped`, or `NotApplicable` for `-SkippedBecause NotApplicable` |
| calls `Add-MtTestResultDetail -SkippedBecause Error`, or throws any error | `Error` | `TestError` |
| returns `$null` without skipping or `-Investigate` | `Skipped` | `NoResult` |
| returns something that is not a boolean, or more than one value | `Error` | `InvalidReturn` |
| runs longer than the configured timeout | `Error` | `Timeout` |

When several apply, they are evaluated in this order: `-SkippedBecause Error`, `-Investigate`, any other
skip, an uncaught error, the returned value.

Watch for stray output. A command whose output you do not capture (`$list.Add($x)` on an `ArrayList`, for
example) adds a second value to the function's output and turns the result into `InvalidReturn`. Assign such
calls to `$null` or pipe them to `Out-Null`.

### Add-MtTestResultDetail

[`Add-MtTestResultDetail`](../commands/Add-MtTestResultDetail.mdx) works as in 2.x. The parameters you use in a
native test:

- `-Result`: the Markdown result. It replaces `%TestResult%` in the `.md` file.
- `-GraphObjects` and `-GraphObjectType`: a list of objects rendered as a table with links to the admin
  portal, inserted where `%TestResult%` appears in `-Result`. See
  [Formatting test results](./formatting-test-results.md).
- `-Investigate`: the result needs a person to look at it.
- `-SkippedBecause`: skip the test for a reason only the test can see, such as `NotApplicable`,
  `NotSupportedAppPermission` or `Custom` with `-SkippedCustomReason`. Do not use the `NotConnected*` and
  `NotLicensed*` codes for conditions the attribute can declare; use `Service` and `License`.
- `-Description`: replaces the description from the `.md` file. Leave it out to use the `.md`.

`-TestTitle` and `-Severity` are ignored in a single-result native test: the title and severity come from the
attribute and the config. In a family, `-TestTitle` sets the instance's title when the instance object has no
`Title`. `-Severity` is used only when neither the config nor the attribute sets one.

### Embedding another tool's report

A test or a family's instance source that runs another tool can embed that tool's own single-file HTML report in
the Maester report with `Add-MtReportAttachment`:

```powershell
Add-MtReportAttachment -Name 'Zero Trust Assessment' -Path "$outputPath/ZeroTrustAssessmentReport.html"
```

The report lists it near the bottom of the left menu (a pack's test's report goes in that pack's menu instead), and shows a button with that name on its overview page and
on the test's result (on every instance of a family). Each opens the embedded report in the main panel, beside the
Maester navigation, with a link to open it in a new browser tab. The attached report runs in a sandboxed frame
without access to the Maester report or its data. It works offline, so the Maester report stays one
file to share. The file is read and compressed at once, so you can delete the tool's output folder afterwards. The JSON
results file lists the attachment's name and size, not its content, and the HTML report leaves HTML attachments out
when `-RedactUserIdentity` is used.

With `-ContentType application/json`, an attachment is data for a view built into the report, which finds it by
its `Name` (the Zero Trust Assessment pack attaches its Zero Trust plan as `zero-trust-workshop`). It is not shown
as a button, and under `-RedactUserIdentity` it is redacted like the results instead of being left out.

### Errors and skips

Do not wrap the body in `try`/`catch` only to report `-SkippedBecause Error`. The engine runs every test inside
its own `try`, so any terminating error ends the test and becomes an `Error` row with the exception message as
`ReasonDetail` and the error record in `ErrorRecord`. Statement-terminating errors (a failed command, a method
call on `$null`) also end the test, so it cannot carry on with empty data and return `$true` by accident.

You may still use `try`/`catch` for a condition you handle, for example a 403 from Graph that you report as
`-SkippedBecause NotAuthorized`. A `-SkippedBecause` call made inside your own `try` block still skips the
test; the engine recognises the skip when your `catch` passes it to `Add-MtTestResultDetail -SkippedBecause
Error -SkippedError $_`.

Warnings and non-terminating errors written by the test are shown on the console and stored on the result row
in `Diagnostics`.

## Declare what the test needs

Do not check connections or licences in the test. Declare them, and the engine decides before the test runs.
A test whose requirement is not met gets a `Skipped` row with a reason code and its `.md` description, so it
still appears in the report. See [Applicability](../configuration/applicability.md) for the order of the
checks and every reason code.

### Service
## Families: one test, several results

Some checks produce one result per item: per drift folder, per recommendation, per user. Declare
`InstanceSource` with the name of a function in the same file. The engine calls that function when the test
runs (never during discovery) and runs the test once per object it returns, passing the object as `$Instance`.

```powershell
function Get-ContosoAdminUnit {
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param()
    foreach ($unit in Invoke-MtGraphRequest -RelativeUri 'directory/administrativeUnits') {
        [pscustomobject]@{
            Id    = $unit.id                     # required: the instance suffix
            Title = "Administrative unit '$($unit.displayName)' is restricted"   # optional
            Data  = $unit                        # optional: anything the test needs
        }
    }
}

function Test-ContosoAdminUnitRestricted {
    [MaesterTest(
        Id = 'CONTOSO.2001',
        Title = 'Administrative units are restricted.',
        Severity = 'Medium',
        Service = 'Graph',
        InstanceSource = 'Get-ContosoAdminUnit'
    )]
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([bool])]
    param(
        # The administrative unit to check, supplied by the engine.
        $Instance
    )

    $restricted = [bool]$Instance.Data.isMemberManagementRestricted
    Add-MtTestResultDetail -Result "Member management restricted: $restricted"
    return $restricted
}
```

The instance object has:

| Property | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Id` | Yes | The suffix. The row's ID is `<parent ID>.<Id>`, for example `CONTOSO.2001.4f6c...`. It must match `^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,127}$` and be unique within the family. |
| `Title` | No | The instance's title. Defaults to `-TestTitle` from the helper, then the attribute's title. |
| `Severity` | No | The instance's severity, used when the config sets none. |
| `Tag` | No | Extra tags written to the instance's row. |
| `Fields` | No | Facts about the instance that a report can group or filter by, as a hashtable of names to strings or arrays of strings, for example `@{ Pillar = 'Identity'; Category = 'Access control' }`. Written to the row's `Fields`; other values are left out. |
| `Product`, `Feature`, `Area`, `RelatedProduct`, `UserImpact`, `ImplementationCost`, `Mitre` | No | What this instance is about, when that differs from its family, with the same keys as the attribute. A family that reads results from another tool, such as the Zero Trust Assessment pack, places each result under its own product this way. A value the taxonomy does not know is left out, and the row keeps the family's. |
| `Data` | No | Anything the test needs. It is not written to the result. |

input.recap: Ten custom tests are in scratch/custom of this worktree, and git ignores that folder locally. A run without a connection made a working report: 1 passed, 8 skipped, 1 error. The Graph checks haven't run against your tenant yet.

content.text:
I wrote 10 custom tests in [scratch/custom](scratch/custom) and checked them with `Get-MtTest -Path`. I only ran them without a tenant connection: that run made a working report with no console errors. The Graph checks haven't run against Pora yet. Git ignores `scratch/` through this worktree's local exclude file, so the folder never shows up as a change.

They're chosen to give the report a mix of results:

| Test | What it checks | Without a connection | Connected |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PORA.1001 | Who can invite guests | Skipped | Pass or fail |
| PORA.1002 | Disabled CA policies state why | Skipped | Pass or fail, with a policy table |
| PORA.1003 | 2–4 Global Admins | Skipped | Pass or fail, with a user table |
| PORA.1004 | Security defaults vs CA | Skipped | Investigate if defaults are on |
| PORA.1005 | Each enabled CA policy excludes break-glass | Skipped | One row per policy (a family) |
| PORA.1006 | Custom domains verified | Skipped | Markdown table of domains |
| PORA.1007 | Teams guest calling | Skipped | Skipped unless Teams is connected |
| PORA.1008 | Runbook owner (needs no tenant) | Passed | Passed |
| PORA.1009 | Directory sync server | Not applicable | Not applicable |
| PORA.1010 | Threat feed file | Error (on purpose) | Error |

They spread across the Entra, Teams and Defender products, plus one test with no product, so the Products menu has a few groups.

To run them, first build and load the module with the new report template:

```bash
cd /Users/merill/github/maester/.claude/worktrees/zero-trust-view && pwsh -NoExit -c "./build/Build-LocalMaester.ps1 -BuildReport"
```

Then, in that PowerShell window, connect and run only the custom tests:

```powershell
Connect-Maester
Invoke-Maester -Path ./scratch/custom -SkipBuiltIn -OutputFolder ./scratch/results
```

The report opens when the run ends and is saved in `scratch/results`. To see Maester's built-in tests too, leave out `-SkipBuiltIn`. To add the Zero Trust pack's results, add `-Pack ZTA`; that starts the full assessment and takes much longer.

`Build-LocalMaester.ps1 -BuildReport` rewrites `powershell/assets/ReportTemplate.html`. That's fine locally, but don't commit it.

cd /Users/merill/github/maester/.claude/worktrees/zero-trust-view/scratch; mkdir -p bare ad
# Bare: only Id and Title
i=0
for spec in "Backup job finished in the last 24 hours|true" "Release branch is protected|true" "Build agents run the latest image|false" "Vendor contract register is up to date|false" "Firewall change log was reviewed this week|investigate" "Office printers have current firmware|true" "Staging certificates expire in more than 30 days|false" "Old VPN profiles are removed|skip"; do
  i=$((i+1)); title="${spec%|*}"; r="${spec#*|}"; id="CHK.$((300+i))"
  case $r in
    true) body="    Add-MtTestResultDetail -Result 'Looks good.'
    return \$true";;
    false) body="    Add-MtTestResultDetail -Result 'This did not meet the bar.'
    return \$false";;
    investigate) body="    Add-MtTestResultDetail -Investigate -Result 'Someone should look at this.'
    return \$false";;
    skip) body="    Add-MtTestResultDetail -SkippedBecause NotApplicable";;
  esac
  cat > bare/Test.$id.ps1 <<EOF
function Test-Chk$((300+i)) {
    [MaesterTest(Id = '$id', Title = '$title')]
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([bool])]
    param()
$body
}
EOF
  printf '%s\n\n<!--- Results --->\n%%TestResult%%\n' "$title." > bare/Test.$id.md
done
# AD-like: Product ad, no Service so they run without a domain
cat > ad/suite.json <<'EOF'
{ "Id": "ContosoAD", "Name": "Contoso Active Directory checks", "Source": "Custom" }
EOF
j=0
for spec in "The KRBTGT password was changed in the last 180 days|domain-and-forest|privileged-access|Critical|false" "Domain controllers run a supported Windows Server version|domain-controllers|infrastructure|High|true" "The AD Recycle Bin is on|domain-and-forest|infrastructure|Medium|true" "No user has a password that never expires|directory-configuration|authentication|High|false" "Domain Admins has no more than five members|directory-configuration|privileged-access|Critical|true" "LDAP signing is required on every domain controller|domain-controllers|authentication|High|investigate" "Unconstrained delegation is not allowed on computers|directory-configuration|privileged-access|Critical|false" "SYSVOL replicates with DFSR|domain-controllers|infrastructure|Low|true"; do
  j=$((j+1)); IFS='|' read -r title feat area sev r <<< "$spec"; id="CAD.$((100+j))"
  case $r in
    true) body="    Add-MtTestResultDetail -Result 'Checked against corp.contoso.com. (Demo data.)'
    return \$true";;
    false) body="    Add-MtTestResultDetail -Result 'Checked against corp.contoso.com: this does not meet the requirement. (Demo data.)'
    return \$false";;
    investigate) body="    Add-MtTestResultDetail -Investigate -Result 'DC02 did not answer the query. (Demo data.)'
    return \$false";;
  esac
  cat > ad/Test.$id.ps1 <<EOF
function Test-Cad$((100+j)) {
    [MaesterTest(Id = '$id', Title = '$title', Product = 'ad', Feature = '$feat', Area = '$area', ResourceType = 'DomainController', Severity = '$sev')]
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([bool])]
    param()
$body
}
EOF
  printf '%s. (Demo data.)\n\n<!--- Results --->\n%%TestResult%%\n' "$title" > ad/Test.$id.md
done
